name: Schola Gentilium

abilities.name: Steady
abilities.text: Improves the unit's ability to defend at the cost of their mobility.

abilities.name: Flying Wedge
abilities.text: The unit moves into a flying wedge-shaped attack formation.

abilities.name: Trample
abilities.text: Charges are more effective for an extended time.

attributes.name: Disciplined
attributes.text: This unit does not suffer a morale penalty when the general dies. It can also rally after routing more often.

attributes.name: Scare (everyone)
attributes.text: This unit frightens all enemy units.

attributes.name: Immune to Fear
attributes.text: This unit is immune to the fear effects of scary units.

short: Scholae Gentilium - the word gentilium can be translated as - stranger (of a foreign tribe). Schola - one of the features of the Later Roman military organization was the creation of new guard units - Scholae Palatinae, which replaced the Praetorian Guard. The latter was finally dissolved by Constantine after his victory over Maxentius. T. Mommsen believed that the scholas were a creation of Constantine. R. Frank attributed this event to the period after 312 AD, after the disbanding of the Praetorian cohorts. In the laws from the Codex Theodosius, it is reported that Constantine granted the right annona civica to two scholae - schola scutariorum and schola clibanariorum, they are considered to be the first scholas. The armament of the scholae differed from the rest of the army. Describing the battle of Argentaria, Ammianus Marcellinus writes that «the shining gold and colorful armor of the imperial guard bent under the frequent blows of throwing projectiles». Despite their military status, the scholae were never under the command of the magister militum and were formally at the disposal of the magister officiorum. Each schola was commanded by a tribune; the tribunes themselves were under the direct command of the Emperor. About number of scholas is judged on a fragment from «Secret History» of Procopius of Caesarea where he writes that during Justinian the imperial palace in Constantinople was guarded by 3,5 thousand scholarians from seven scholae. That is, the number of one schola was about 500 men.
history: One of the simplest forms of one-armed catapult, the onager relied on twisted skeins of animal sinew which provided the power to hurl either rocks or shot. Inaccurate but powerful, it was an effective siege machine against buildings and fortifications, but was of far less use on the battlefield unless firing into massed infantry ranks. First mentioned by Philon of Byzantium in his treatise on ‘Mechanics’, the onager made use of a sling-like cradle attached to a firing arm. This arm was inserted, twisted, and propelled rocks or shot through torsion. As the firing arm was released, the sling-like cradle would unhook, firing the projectile. A padded beam was incorporated into the housing frame to restrain the arm. Larger machines could require as many as eight or ten crewmen, and the incredible recoil meant that they could not be easily or safely mounted on walls or towers. Quickly constructed wherever wood was readily available, onagers soon became a staple of ancient siege warfare.
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
